Notes: Year Established basis: earliest literary claim of a Jewish community at Ephesus. Josephus (Contra Apionem 2.4 [2.39]; cf. Ant. 12.125-126) says the Jews of Ephesus and Ionia held citizenship granted by the Diadochi; the Greeks themselves credited Antiochus II Theos (261-246 BCE), so the Jewish Encyclopedia concludes equal rights probably date from his reign. Year = midpoint of the reign (c.). Presence only, no count. Caution: Trebilco (Durham PhD 1987, pp. 190-193) and Tcherikover doubt Josephus' citizenship claims, so the date of first settlement is uncertain; the first securely datable documents are of 49 BCE.

Decree of the consul L. Lentulus Crus (Josephus, Ant. 14.10.13 [14.228]; repeated 14.234, 14.240), dated 'before the twelfth of the calends of October' in the consulship of Lentulus and Marcellus (=49 BCE): Jews who are Roman citizens and follow Jewish rites 'and yet live at Ephesus' exempted from military service. Documents an organized Jewish community at Ephesus including Roman citizens; no number. Ancient documentary source.

Scholarly assessment of the 49 BCE Lentulus exemption (Ant. 14.228-240), Trebilco, Studies on Jewish Communities in Asia Minor (Durham PhD 1987), ch. 1 sec. 5.4 and ch. 3 sec. 2.1: Lentulus was raising two legions in Asia; the exemption covered Jewish Roman citizens practising at Ephesus (and, per the legate's letter Ant. 14.230 and confirmation by propraetor C. Fannius, the Jews of Asia). Smallwood held the number affected was 'infinitesimally small' but that the gesture aimed at 'the large and influential Jewish communities in Asia'; Safrai and Stern say of the Ephesian community 'Quite a number of them were Roman citizens'; Tcherikover speaks of 'a considerable group'. Trebilco: the matter cannot be decided. Indicates a substantial community; no numeric estimate, so Population blank.

Letter of P. Cornelius Dolabella, imperator (governor of Syria; Josephus wrongly calls him prefect of Asia), to the magistrates, council and people of Ephesus, dated in the prytany of Artemon, 43 BCE (Josephus, Ant. 14.10.12 [14.225-227]): at the request of Hyrcanus II's envoy Alexander son of Theodorus, Jews exempted from military service because they cannot bear arms or march on the Sabbath or obtain their ancestral foods, and allowed to assemble for sacred rites and collect offerings. Presence of an organized community; no count.

Decree of the people of Ephesus (Josephus, Ant. 14.10.25 [14.262-264]; prytanis Menophilus, 1 Artemision): the Jews of the city petitioned the proconsul (text 'Marcus Julius Pompeius son of Brutus', probably M. Junius Brutus, in Asia early 42 BCE) to keep their Sabbaths and ancestral customs; the city decreed no one should hinder or fine them. Dated 42 BCE by this source (Trebilco 1987 also: 'perhaps to be dated to 42 BCE'; COJS places it in the 47-42 BCE series). Trebilco notes Jews at Ephesus seem to have been prevented from and fined for keeping the Sabbath around 42 BCE. Presence; no count.

Letter of the proconsul C. Norbanus Flaccus 'to the governors of the Ephesians' (Philo, Legatio ad Gaium 40 [315]): Caesar (Augustus) wrote that Jews everywhere assemble and collect money to send to Jerusalem; they are to be allowed to do so. Trebilco (1987, ch.1 n.116) dates Leg. 315-316 to 18-12 BCE; year = midpoint (c.). Indicates a community collecting Temple dues; no count.

Letter of M. Agrippa to the magistrates, council and people of the Ephesians (Josephus, Ant. 16.6.4 [16.167-168]): custody of the sacred money sent to the Temple in Jerusalem left to the Jews of Asia according to ancestral custom; thieves of it treated as temple-robbers; Jews not to be compelled to appear in court on the Sabbath. Date: Agrippa was in the East 23-21 and 16-13 BCE; Trebilco (1987) links the Sabbath-court issue to 14 BCE, the year of Nicolaus of Damascus' defence of the Ionian Jews before Agrippa (Ant. 16.27-61). Year c. 14 BCE. Presence; no count.

Event: under Augustus the Ephesians (with other Ionians) demanded that if the Jews were their equals they should worship the city's gods; Nicolaus of Damascus defended the Jews before M. Agrippa, who confirmed their right to live by their own customs (Josephus, Ant. 12.125-126; 16.27-61). Year: the Jewish Encyclopedia gives '10 B.C.' for Agrippa's governance of the East, but Agrippa was in the East 16-13 BCE and Nicolaus' defence is usually dated 14 BCE (Trebilco 1987), so -14 is used (c.). Indicates an established community in civic conflict with the Greek citizens; no count.

Letter of the proconsul Julius Antonius to the magistrates, council and people of the Ephesians, written while 'dispensing justice at Ephesus, on the Ides of February' (Josephus, Ant. 16.6.7 [16.172-173]): the Jews of Asia asked him to confirm the rights granted by Augustus and Agrippa to follow their laws and send first-fruits to Jerusalem. Trebilco (1987, n.126) dates it between 9 and 2 BCE; year = midpoint (c.). Presence; no count.

Regional context only: 'Several scholars have estimated a substantial Jewish population in Asia Minor by the first century CE, perhaps as much as 10-15 percent of the total population' - a regional share for Asia Minor, NOT a figure for Ephesus, so Population blank. The same page says the Ephesian community is thought to have originated among soldiers or captives relocated to the city. Year = 1st c. CE midpoint.

Acts 18:19-26: Paul 'went into the synagogue and had a discussion with the Jews' at Ephesus; then the Alexandrian Jew Apollos 'began to speak boldly in the synagogue' and was instructed by the Jewish couple Priscilla and Aquila. Synagogue congregation attested; no count. Date c. 52 CE per conventional Pauline chronology (not stated in the text).

Acts 19: Paul spoke in the Ephesus synagogue for three months (19:8), then moved to the hall of Tyrannus; 'itinerant Jewish exorcists' including 'seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva' (19:13-14); during the riot of the silversmiths the Jews pushed forward Alexander, recognized as a Jew (19:33-34). Shows a synagogue community and a publicly identifiable Jewish group in the city; no count. Date c. 53-55 CE per conventional chronology (c.; not stated in the text).
